opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it is that we don't think we know all the answers yet. When you put an agent in someone's terminal, right next to their code, the range of things people want to do with it is enormous, and no single team is going to anticipate all of it. Open-sourcing it is a way of saying, "Here's the foundation. Take it, bend it, make it fit your workflow."

Concretely, there are a few things I'm excited about. First, people can just look under the hood. Agents can feel a bit magical and a bit opaque. When you can read the code, see how the prompts are put together, how tool calls get made, how sandboxing and approvals work, you build intuition for how these systems behave. That makes you better at using them and better at building your own.

Second, customization. Every engineering org has its own conventions, internal tools, and deployment quirks. We'd love to see people wire Codex CLI into their own environments: hooking it up to internal tooling, adding custom commands, building workflows specific to their codebase. Those aren't things we could build for everyone, but they're easy to build once you have the source.

Third, and this is the most interesting one to me, I hope people use it as a starting point for entirely new agents. The core loop is surprisingly general: a model that can read context, take actions, observe results, and iterate. Coding is a great first domain because the feedback is crisp. Tests pass or they don't, the code runs or it doesn't. But I'd love to see people take that loop into data analysis, infrastructure, research workflows, things we haven't thought of.

And selfishly, it makes the product better. The community finds the rough edges faster than we ever could, and a lot of the best ideas will come from people using it in ways we didn't expect. So the hope is that it becomes less "our tool" and more a shared foundation the community builds on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses customizing Codex CLI for internal tools and workflows, but does not identify using it in CI to automatically attempt repairs when builds or tests fail.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know, and that's kind of the point. When we were building Codex CLI internally, we kept running into this thing where the model was clearly capable of a lot more than the interface we'd wrapped around it was letting people do. And every time we'd add a feature, someone would come back and say, "Okay, but what I actually want is this slightly different thing." Open-sourcing it is partly an admission that the long tail of what people want to do with an agent in their terminal is way bigger than what one team can anticipate.

So concretely, a few categories I'm excited about. The first is just integration into workflows we haven't thought about. The CLI is a pretty thin layer between the model and your local environment, and that environment could be a monorepo at a big company with its own build system, or a data scientist's notebook setup, or some embedded systems workflow where the tooling is really idiosyncratic. People who live in those environments know way better than we do how an agent should plug in, and now they can actually go change the code instead of filing a feature request and waiting.

The second thing is the agent loop itself. Right now there's a particular way we handle things like when to run a command versus ask for approval, how we present diffs, how we manage context when a task runs long. Those are all design decisions, and reasonable people will disagree with them. I'd love to see people experiment with different approaches to safety and approval, different ways of structuring multi-step tasks, maybe different ways of having multiple agents cooperate. Some of that will be better than what we shipped, and we'll learn from it.

And then the third thing, which is maybe the most interesting to me, is that the CLI becomes a building block rather than an end product. If you think about how a lot of software gets written, there are these repetitive, well-defined tasks: migrating off a deprecated API, adding test coverage, fixing lint errors across a huge codebase. I think people are going to build higher-level tools on top of this that encode their team's conventions and run these kinds of jobs semi-autonomously. That's where I think the real leverage is, and it's not something we can build for every team ourselves.

The other piece, which is a little less about what people build and more about trust, is that if you're going to let an agent run commands on your machine, you should be able to read the code that's doing it. I think that matters a lot for adoption, especially in more security-conscious environments.

r001.rationale: The response mentions integrating Codex CLI into varied workflows and automating repetitive code tasks, but does not identify using it in CI to repair build or test failures.

astra-6.text: My hope is that people take it in directions we wouldn’t have thought of. A coding agent needs to fit into the way you actually work—your tools, your environment, the conventions of your team. Open-sourcing the CLI gives developers a way to experiment with those things directly, whether that’s adding integrations, changing how the agent interacts with them, or building a different workflow around it. I’m excited to see what people find useful and to learn from that.

By open-sourcing Codex CLI, we’re giving people something they can inspect, modify, and build on—whether that means connecting it to their own tools, adapting it to their codebase, or experimenting with a different way of working with an agent.
